• PCB GM levels varied across participating regions with highest levels in the Sahtú and Dehcho regions and lower levels in Old Crow • Determinants of PCB biomarkers differed across participating regions • Those aged 60+ showed higher PCB exposure levels for certain congeners in the Dehcho and the Sahtú regions compared to the CHMS • This research contributes to information on contaminant risk assessments in northern environments will inform future environmental monitoring efforts • Future work will look at possible sources of PCB exposure from Food Frequency Questionnaires Persistent organic pollutants (POPs) including polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) can be found in Arctic and sub-arctic regions of Canada due to long-range transport and local point sources. Though there have been several national biomonitoring programs that have recorded PCB exposure levels (e.g., Canadian Health Measures Survey (CHMS) and the First Nations Biomonitoring Initiative (FNBI)), no recent data exists describing exposure levels in the Northwest Territories (NWT) and Yukon.

The aim of this study was to collect and report contaminant exposure levels and other nutrient biomarkers including omega-3 fatty acids (DHA+EPA) because PCBs and other POPs are lipophilic in nature; thus omega-3 fatty acids may co-vary with exposure levels. The study was conducted between the years 2016-2019 from two regions in the Northwest Territories and from one community in the Yukon to fill a human biomonitoring data gap in Canada. This study was done in partnership with local communities and leaders.

Participants by age and sex for those who provided blood samples Descriptive statistics were generated using SPSS (e.g., Geometric means, percentiles, detection limits), and statistical analyses were conducted (e.g., independent samples T-test, Spearman’s rho) to assess associations between variables including omega-3 fatty acids, sex and region.
Twenty-four PCB congeners, 1 mixture and 4 PCB groupings were then lipid-adjusted Samples (plasma for PCBs) were analyzed through gas chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry.

Biomonitoring clinics were established throughout the communities where hair, blood and urine samples were collected for contaminant and omega-3 fatty acid analysis. Demographic data and dietary patterns were also collected.
Community outreach took place and consultations began to create a series of Community Research Agreements.
